microservices-basics.tldr:
• Microservices trade code complexity for network, data and operational complexity.
  • Benefits: independent deploys, targeted scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy.
  • Start with a modular monolith; extract services when scaling, cadence or ownership demands it.
  • Migrate incrementally with the strangler fig pattern.
microservices-basics.body:
A microservice is an independently deployable service that owns one business capability and its own data, communicating over the network.

Monolith Microservices
Deploy one unit each service independently
Scale whole app per service
Data one shared DB, ACID transactions DB per service, eventual consistency
Failure one bug can crash all isolated, but partial failures everywhere
Complexity in the code in the network, ops and data
Team fit small team many autonomous teams (Conway's law)

Benefits: independent deploys and release cadence, targeted scaling, fault isolation, technology freedom, team autonomy.

Costs: network latency and failures, distributed transactions, data consistency, operational overhead (CI/CD per service, observability, service mesh), harder testing and debugging.

Interview tip say you'd start with a modular monolith (clear module boundaries, one deployable) and extract services when a module needs independent scaling, release cadence or team ownership. Microservices are an organizational scaling tool as much as a technical one.

Strangler fig migration: put a routing layer (API gateway) in front of the monolith; build new functionality as services; route specific paths to them; gradually carve out modules; retire the monolith. Use an anti-corruption layer to translate between old and new models.

Modular monolith in practice: one deployable, but each module has its own package root, a public API (interfaces/events), its own tables, and enforced boundaries (Spring Modulith or ArchUnit tests that fail the build when orders reaches into payments.internal). Extraction later is then a mechanical change.

microservices-decomposition.tldr:
• Split by business capability and bounded context, not by technical layer.
  • An aggregate is the unit of consistency: one transaction modifies one aggregate.
  • Each service owns its data; others use its API or events.
  • Smells of a distributed monolith: lockstep deploys, chatty sync chains, shared tables.
microservices-decomposition.body:
Split by business capability, not by technical layer. Domain-Driven Design helps find boundaries:

  • Bounded context: a boundary within which a model and its language are consistent. "Product" means something different to Catalog (description, images), Inventory (stock, warehouse) and Pricing (price lists).
  • Aggregate: a cluster of entities with one root that enforces invariants and is the unit of consistency (one transaction modifies one aggregate). Order (root) with OrderLines.
  • Ubiquitous language: shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts.
  • Context map: how contexts relate (customer/supplier, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel, published language).

A context map for an e-commerce domain

The same word means different things in each context, and that's fine: each service has its own Product model, and they share only identifiers and published events.

Aggregate rules (Vaughn Vernon): design small aggregates; reference other aggregates by id, not object reference; one transaction modifies one aggregate; use eventual consistency (events) between aggregates. An Order holds customerId, not a Customer object.

Good service boundaries: high cohesion inside, loose coupling across; services can be deployed without coordinating with others; few synchronous calls between them; each owns its data.

Smells of a bad split (distributed monolith): services must be deployed together; chatty synchronous call chains (A → B → C → D for one request); shared database tables; one change touches five services.

Database per service: each service owns its schema; others access the data only through its API or events. Patterns for cross-service queries: API composition, CQRS read models, and data replication via events.

microservices-communication.tldr:
• Sync (REST/gRPC) for queries and immediate answers; async (Kafka/RabbitMQ) for events, workflows and spikes.
  • Events state facts; commands ask a specific service to act.
  • Declarative HTTP clients (@HttpExchange) keep calls typed; always configure timeouts.
  • Evolve APIs additively with tolerant readers.

microservices-gateway.tldr:
• The gateway centralizes routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS and canary routing; BFFs tailor responses per client.
  • Discovery is client-side (Eureka) or server-side (Kubernetes Services).
  • Centralize configuration (Config Server, ConfigMaps) and refresh safely.
  • A service mesh moves mTLS, retries and telemetry into sidecars.
microservices-gateway.body:
API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway): single entry point that handles routing, authentication (validate JWT once), rate limiting, CORS, request aggregation, TLS termination, canary routing. BFF (Backend for Frontend): one gateway per client type (web, mobile) shaping responses for it.

YAML
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: lb://order-service              # load-balanced via discovery
          predicates: [ Path=/api/orders/** ]
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=1
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args: { name: ordersCb, fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/orders }

Service discovery: instances register themselves; clients find healthy instances.

  • Client-side (Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer): client fetches the list and picks an instance.
  • Server-side (Kubernetes Services, AWS ALB): client calls a stable DNS name; the platform load-balances. On Kubernetes you rarely need Eureka.

Centralized configuration: Spring Cloud Config Server (Git-backed), Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets, Consul, AWS Parameter Store. Refresh at runtime with @RefreshScope or by rolling pods.

Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd): a sidecar proxy per pod handles mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry outside your code.

microservices-resilience.tldr:
• Every remote call needs a timeout; slow dependencies are worse than dead ones.
  • Retry only transient errors on idempotent calls, with exponential backoff and jitter, at one layer.
  • Circuit breakers fail fast (CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN); bulkheads isolate dependencies.
  • Provide fallbacks: cached data, defaults or degraded responses.

microservices-saga.tldr:
• A Saga is a chain of local transactions with compensating actions instead of 2PC.
  • Choreography suits short flows; orchestration suits long flows with timeouts.
  • Every step and compensation must be idempotent.
  • Intermediate states are visible: model them (PENDING) and use semantic locks.

microservices-outbox.tldr:
• Writing to the DB and a broker separately can diverge (dual write).
  • Outbox: write the event in the same transaction; a relay or Debezium CDC publishes it.
  • Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event id.
  • Key events by aggregate id to keep per-entity order.
microservices-outbox.body:
The dual-write problem: you save an order to the database and publish OrderCreated to Kafka. If the app crashes between the two, or one fails, the systems disagree. You can't make the DB and Kafka atomic together.

Outbox pattern: write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business data. A separate relay publishes outbox rows to the broker.

Java
@Transactional
public Order placeOrder(CreateOrderRequest req) {
    Order order = orderRepo.save(Order.from(req));
    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent(
        UUID.randomUUID(), "Order", order.getId().toString(),
        "OrderCreated", json.write(OrderCreated.of(order))));
    return order;                        // both rows commit atomically or neither does
}

// Relay option A: polling publisher
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
public void relay() {
    for (OutboxEvent e : outboxRepo.findTop100ByPublishedFalseOrderByCreatedAt()) {
        kafka.send("orders", e.aggregateId(), e.payload()).join();   // key = aggregate id keeps order
        e.markPublished();
        outboxRepo.save(e);
    }
}
// Relay option B (preferred at scale): CDC with Debezium tails the DB log and publishes
// outbox rows to Kafka with no polling and no extra load on the table.

Outbox table design

SQL
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type text        NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id   text        NOT NULL,
  event_type     text        NOT NULL,
  payload        jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at   timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;
-- Multiple relay instances: claim rows without blocking each other
SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Purge published rows regularly (or partition by day and drop old partitions). With Debezium you can even delete the row in the same transaction: the insert is still in the WAL and gets published.

The relay gives at-least-once delivery (it can publish and crash before marking), so consumers must be idempotent.

Idempotent consumer: record processed message IDs in the same transaction as the side effect.

Java
@Transactional
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
public void handle(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) {
    String eventId = new String(rec.headers().lastHeader("eventId").value());
    if (processedRepo.existsById(eventId)) return;          // duplicate: skip
    billing.createInvoice(json.read(rec.value(), OrderCreated.class));
    processedRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(eventId));        // unique constraint as a last guard
}

Inbox pattern is the mirror image: store incoming messages first, process them from the table.

microservices-cqrs.tldr:
• CQRS separates the write model from denormalized read models updated by events.
  • Use it when read and write shapes or loads differ greatly, not for simple CRUD.
  • Event sourcing stores events as the source of truth and rebuilds state by replay with snapshots.
  • Costs: eventual consistency, schema evolution of events, projections to query.
microservices-cqrs.body:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): separate the write model (commands, enforcing invariants, normalized) from the read model (queries, denormalized views optimized per screen). The read side is updated from events, so it is eventually consistent.

Handle the read-your-own-writes problem: after a command, return the new state from the write side, or have the client poll with the command's version until the read model has caught up.

Use it when read and write loads or shapes differ a lot, e.g. an order service writes to Postgres and publishes events that build an Elasticsearch search index and a Redis "order summary" view. Don't use it for simple CRUD.

Event Sourcing: instead of storing current state, store the sequence of events (OrderCreated, ItemAdded, OrderPaid). Current state = replaying the events (with periodic snapshots for speed).

Java
public class Account {
    private BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO;
    private final List<Event> changes = new ArrayList<>();

    public static Account rehydrate(List<Event> history) {
        Account a = new Account();
        history.forEach(a::apply);
        return a;
    }
    public void withdraw(BigDecimal amt) {
        if (balance.compareTo(amt) < 0) throw new InsufficientFunds();   // invariant check
        raise(new MoneyWithdrawn(amt));
    }
    private void raise(Event e) { apply(e); changes.add(e); }
    private void apply(Event e) {
        switch (e) {
            case MoneyDeposited d -> balance = balance.add(d.amount());
            case MoneyWithdrawn w -> balance = balance.subtract(w.amount());
            default -> { }
        }
    }
}

Benefits: complete audit log, temporal queries ("balance on March 1"), rebuild new read models any time. Costs: event schema evolution, eventual consistency, a learning curve, and querying requires projections.

microservices-observability.tldr:
• Correlate logs, metrics and traces with a trace id.
  • Metrics: RED per endpoint, USE per resource; alert on SLOs.
  • Traces show which hop is slow; context propagates through HTTP headers and Kafka headers.
  • Use structured JSON logs and sample traces sensibly.
microservices-observability.body:
In a request that crosses eight services, you need three signals correlated by a trace id:

  • Logs: structured JSON with traceId, spanId, service, and business ids. Ship to Loki/ELK.
  • Metrics: RED per endpoint (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). Prometheus + Grafana, alerts on SLOs.
  • Traces: a span per hop showing where the time went. OpenTelemetry → Tempo/Jaeger/Zipkin.

What a trace shows

The waterfall immediately shows the inventory reservation (mostly a lock wait) dominating the request, something no single service's logs would reveal.

YAML
# Spring Boot 3 + Micrometer Tracing (OpenTelemetry bridge)
management:
  tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0      # lower in prod, or use tail sampling in the collector
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"

Context propagates via the W3C traceparent header over HTTP and as Kafka record headers. Instrumented clients (RestClient, WebClient, KafkaTemplate with observation enabled) do this automatically.

Correlation id vs trace id: a trace id is generated by tracing and spans the whole call tree; a business correlation id (order id) helps support teams search logs.

microservices-deployment.tldr:
• Rolling, blue/green, canary and feature flags trade cost against blast radius and rollback speed.
  • Readiness removes a pod from traffic; liveness restarts it — never check dependencies in liveness.
  • Services must be stateless to scale horizontally.
  • Follow twelve-factor: config in env, disposability, logs as streams.
microservices-deployment.body:
Deployment strategies

Database migrations with zero downtime (expand / contract): during a rolling update, old and new versions run at the same time against one schema, so every migration must be compatible with both.

Strategy How Rollback Cost
Rolling update replace pods gradually redeploy previous version none extra
Blue-green full new environment, switch traffic at once switch back instantly double resources
Canary small % of traffic to new version, increase on good metrics shift traffic back low
Feature flags deploy dark, enable per user flip the flag flag management

Kubernetes essentials for Spring services

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy: { rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 } }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry/order-service:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "768Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "768Mi" }
          env:
            - { name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
          lifecycle:
            preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] } }   # let endpoints deregister
  • Readiness removes a pod from load balancing (warming up, dependency down); liveness restarts it (deadlocked). Don't put downstream dependencies in liveness, or one DB blip restarts every pod.
  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU or custom metrics (Kafka lag via KEDA).
  • Services must be stateless to scale horizontally: sessions in Redis, files in object storage.
  • Twelve-Factor App: config in env, stateless processes, disposability (fast start, graceful shutdown), dev/prod parity, logs as streams.

qa.q: What are the main challenges of microservices?
qa.a: Distributed data and consistency (no cross-service ACID), network failures and latency, cascading failures, observability across services, testing and versioning contracts, operational overhead (many pipelines, deployments, configs), and organizational alignment.

qa.q: How do services communicate, and how do you choose?
qa.a: Synchronous REST/gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer (queries, user-facing reads). Asynchronous messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for events, long workflows, fan-out and load leveling. Prefer async between services for writes to reduce temporal coupling, and keep sync call chains short.

qa.q: How do you handle distributed transactions?
qa.a: Avoid them by designing boundaries around aggregates. When a flow spans services, use a Saga with compensating transactions (choreography for simple flows, orchestration for complex ones), the transactional outbox to publish events reliably, and idempotent consumers. 2PC is avoided due to blocking and availability cost.

It wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures. CLOSED: calls pass. When the failure or slow-call rate exceeds a threshold, it goes OPEN: calls fail immediately (fallback) without hitting the dependency, giving it time to recover. After a wait it goes HALF_OPEN and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it, failure reopens it.

qa.q: What is the dual-write problem and how does the Outbox pattern solve it?
qa.a: Writing to the DB and publishing to a broker are two separate systems; a crash between them causes inconsistency. Outbox writes the event to a table in the same DB transaction as the state change, then a relay (poller or Debezium CDC) publishes it. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate.

qa.q: What is an API gateway and why use one?
qa.a: A single entry point that routes requests to services and centralizes cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, TLS, CORS, logging, request aggregation and canary routing, so services and clients stay simpler.

Instances register with a registry (Eureka, Consul) or the platform tracks them (Kubernetes endpoints). Clients resolve a logical name to healthy instances, either client-side (fetch list, load-balance locally) or server-side (DNS name behind a load balancer). Health checks remove dead instances.

No, by default. A shared schema couples deployments and data models and makes ownership unclear. Each service owns its data; others use its API or subscribe to its events. Shared DB is acceptable only as a transitional step during migration.

qa.q: How do you ensure idempotency in APIs and consumers?
qa.a: For APIs: an Idempotency-Key header stored with the result (unique constraint); repeated requests return the stored response. For consumers: track processed event IDs in the same transaction as the side effect, use natural upserts, or version checks. Design operations as "set state to X" rather than "increment".

Choreography: each service listens for events and emits new ones; loosely coupled but the overall flow is implicit and hard to monitor. Orchestration: a coordinator sends commands and tracks state; explicit, easier to handle timeouts and compensation, but adds a central component.

Splitting the write model (commands, invariants) from read models (denormalized views per query) updated asynchronously from events. It allows independent scaling and optimized queries at the cost of eventual consistency and complexity.

qa.q: How would you debug a slow request across 6 services?
qa.a: Find the trace by trace id (from logs or the gateway), look at the span waterfall to locate the slow hop, then drill into that service's metrics (latency percentiles, thread/connection pool saturation, GC) and logs filtered by trace id. Check for sequential calls that could be parallel, retries, N+1 queries and missing timeouts.

qa.q: What is the strangler fig pattern?
qa.a: An incremental migration: put a facade/gateway in front of the monolith, implement new or extracted features as services, and route matching traffic to them, slowly shrinking the monolith until it can be retired, with no big-bang rewrite.

qa.q: What's the difference between liveness and readiness probes?
qa.a: Readiness says "can I take traffic now?"; failing it removes the pod from the Service endpoints without restarting. Liveness says "am I broken beyond recovery?"; failing it restarts the container. Keep liveness local (no external dependency checks).

qa.q: How do you version APIs without breaking clients?
qa.a: Make additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, tolerant readers). For breaking changes, introduce a new version (URI or media type), run both, migrate consumers, deprecate with a timeline. Consumer-driven contract tests (Spring Cloud Contract, Pact) catch breaks before deploy.

  • Metrics: RED per endpoint, USE per resource; alert on SLOs.

  • Use structured JSON logs and sample traces sensibly.

  • Rolling, blue/green, canary and feature flags trade cost against blast radius and rollback speed.
